source.title: Letters to His Son
authors: Philip Dormer Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
source.attribution: Philip Dormer Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield, Letters to His Son, Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: Good manners are what make your ability welcome
cards.body:
Chesterfield told his son that solid knowledge was the foundation of his future, but that knowledge alone would not carry him far. He compared it to a great rough diamond: valuable, but it will never be worn or shine until it is polished. Manners are the polish.

The same is true at work and among friends today. Two people can know the same things, yet the one who listens, greets people warmly and explains without talking down is the one others want to work with. Skill gets you considered; courtesy gets you welcomed.
cards.quote: But remember, that manners must adorn knowledge, and smooth its way through the world.
cards.apply_it: Think of a skill you are proud of. Ask yourself whether the way you share it makes people glad to come to you.

quiz.question: What image did Chesterfield use for knowledge without manners?
options: A rough diamond that is never worn
quiz.explanation: Knowledge without manners is like a rough diamond: it has value, but it will not shine until it is polished.

cards.title: Small attentions decide whether people like you
cards.body:
Answering a letter, returning a call, remembering a friend's request: Chesterfield called these attentions that cost little and please a great deal. Great merit or great failings, he said, make people respect or despise you. But whether they like or dislike you mostly comes down to trifles, done or neglected.

He suggested a simple test. Ask yourself why you like some people and not others, and you will usually find the reasons are small. A quick reply, a thank-you note or a question about someone's weekend are easy to give and surprisingly easy to forget.
cards.quote: Those attentions ought never to be omitted; they cost little, and please a great deal; but the neglect of them offends more than you can yet imagine.
cards.apply_it: Reply today to one message you have been putting off, even if only to say you will answer properly soon.

quiz.question: According to Chesterfield, what mostly decides whether people like or dislike you?
quiz.explanation: Great merit earns respect, but liking comes from small attentions that cost little and please a great deal.

cards.title: Notice what pleases you in others, then offer it
cards.body:
The art of pleasing, Chesterfield admitted, can hardly be reduced to rules. His surest method was the oldest one: do as you would be done by. Watch what pleases you in other people, he said, and the same thing in you will probably please them.

If you feel cared for when someone remembers your tastes or makes allowance for your weak spots, others will feel the same when you do it for them. Your own reactions are a free, daily guide to good manners. You only have to pay attention to them.
cards.quote: Observe carefully what pleases you in others, and probably the same thing in you will please others.
cards.apply_it: Recall the last time someone made you feel genuinely welcome. Name exactly what they did, and do it for someone this week.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield call the surest method of pleasing people?
options: Doing as you would be done by
quiz.explanation: He recommended the golden rule: watch what pleases you in others and offer the same.

cards.title: Do one thing at a time, and do not put it off
cards.body:
Chesterfield told the story of a Dutch statesman, De Witt, who ran the business of a whole republic yet still had evenings free for company. Asked how, he said it was easy: he did only one thing at a time and never put off till tomorrow what could be done today.

Chesterfield saw this steady, undivided attention as a mark of real ability, and hurry and bustle as a sign of a scattered mind. Today, with every screen pulling at us, single-tasking is still the quiet secret behind people who get a lot done and still seem relaxed.
cards.quote: it was only doing one thing at a time, and never putting off anything till to-morrow that could be done to-day.
cards.apply_it: Pick your most important task for tomorrow. Close every other tab and app for the first half hour you spend on it.

quiz.question: How did the statesman in Chesterfield's story manage so much business and still enjoy his evenings?
options: He did one thing at a time and did not delay
quiz.explanation: He said it was easy: do only one thing at a time and never put off what could be done today.

cards.title: When you are with people, be with them
cards.body:
Chesterfield had little patience for the 'absent man' who drifts off in company, forgets the people he chatted with yesterday, and breaks into the conversation as if waking from a dream. A Newton or a Locke deep in great problems might be excused, he said, but most of us cannot claim that.

Even if a gathering feels dull, showing that you think so is a small insult, and people forgive insults less easily than injuries. Today the phone on the table does the same thing. Being fully present is one of the simplest courtesies you can offer.
cards.quote: However frivolous a company may be, still, while you are among them, do not show them, by your inattention, that you think them so
cards.apply_it: At your next meal with others, put your phone out of sight and see what you notice about the people with you.

quiz.question: Why did Chesterfield dislike 'absent' behaviour in company?
options: It shows people you think them not worth your attention
It makes you look too clever
quiz.explanation: Inattention tells people you think them frivolous, and that kind of slight is remembered.

cards.title: Look at the person speaking to you, not around the room
cards.body:
Of all the ways to give offence, Chesterfield thought few were as little forgiven as seeming not to listen. He described people who, while you speak, stare at the ceiling, look out of the window, play with a dog or fiddle with a snuff-box. Their message is plain: anything in the room deserves more attention than you.

He asked his son to be not only attentive but visibly attentive to whoever spoke to him. Today the snuff-box is a phone, but the effect is the same. Eye contact, a nod and a relevant question tell someone they matter.
cards.quote: There is nothing so brutally shocking, nor so little forgiven, as a seeming inattention to the person who is speaking to you
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation, keep your eyes on the speaker and ask one follow-up question about what they just said.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield say seeming inattention tells the speaker?
options: That you are busy and important
That any trifling object deserves your attention more than they do
quiz.explanation: Looking elsewhere declares that even the smallest object in the room matters more than the person talking.

cards.title: Take care of the minutes and the hours look after themselves
cards.body:
Chesterfield borrowed a miser's saying, take care of the pence and the pounds will take care of themselves, and turned it to time. Look after the minutes, he told his son, and the hours will follow. He was sure many people lose two or three hours a day simply by ignoring the small gaps.

No stretch of time is too short to use, he said; something can always be done in it. Ten minutes before a meeting, a wait for the bus or a gap between tasks can hold a short read, a quick note or a reply that clears your list.
cards.quote: I recommend to you to take care of the minutes; for hours will take care of themselves.
cards.apply_it: List three small things you could do in a five-minute gap. Keep the list handy for the next time you are waiting.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield adapt the miser's saying about pence and pounds into?
options: Save your money for old age
Take care of the minutes and the hours will take care of themselves
quiz.explanation: He applied the miser's thrift to time: minded minutes add up to well-used hours.

cards.title: Keep light, useful reading for the spare moments of the day
cards.body:
Chesterfield, with a smile, praised a gentleman who read his way through the Latin poets a couple of pages at a time in the few minutes he spent each day in the privy. The point was serious. Grave books of science need continuous attention, he said, but many good books can be read in snatches.

Poems, short essays and reference books fit neatly into the little idle intervals everyone has. Keep something worthwhile within reach, on the shelf or on your phone, and short waits become steady reading over a year.
cards.quote: Books of science, and of a grave sort, must be read with continuity; but there are very many, and even very useful ones, which may be read with advantage by snatches, and unconnectedly
cards.apply_it: Put a book of short pieces, such as poems or essays, where you usually wait or scroll, and read one piece there today.

quiz.question: Which kind of books did Chesterfield say must be read with continuity?
options: Books of science and a grave sort
quiz.explanation: Serious, systematic books need steady reading, while poems and reference works can be enjoyed in snatches.

cards.title: End each day by asking whether you used it or squandered it
cards.body:
Late in life Chesterfield wished that every thinking person would ask a few questions at bedtime. What have I done today? Was any of it useful to me or to others? Did I use my time, or squander it? Did I live the day, or doze it away?

He observed that work done well lifts the mind, while idleness lets it stagnate. A short evening review is still one of the simplest habits you can build. It is not about guilt. It is about noticing, so that tomorrow goes a little more the way you intend.
cards.quote: Have I employed my time, or have I squandered it?
cards.apply_it: Tonight before bed, write one line answering: what did I do today that was useful to me or to someone else?

quiz.question: Which question did Chesterfield wish people would ask themselves each night?
options: How much did I earn today?
Have I employed my time, or have I squandered it?
quiz.explanation: He hoped every rational person would ask at bedtime whether they had used the day or wasted it.

cards.title: Talk often, but never for long
cards.body:
Chesterfield opened his rules for conversation with a short one: talk often, but never long. If you do not please, at least you will not tire anyone. He added a gentle joke: pay your own share of the conversation, but do not try to pay for the whole table, because nobody likes to be treated that way in talk.

In meetings and at dinner, the people others enjoy are rarely those who hold the floor longest. Short, frequent contributions leave room for everyone else and keep people wanting to hear what you will say next.
cards.quote: Talk often, but never long: in that case, if you do not please, at least you are sure not to tire your hearers.
cards.apply_it: In your next group conversation, keep each turn to a few sentences and then hand the floor back with a question.

quiz.question: What was Chesterfield's reasoning behind 'talk often, but never long'?
options: Even if you do not please, you will not tire your listeners
quiz.explanation: Short turns protect your listeners from boredom, even when what you say is not brilliant.

cards.title: Tell stories rarely, and only short ones that fit
cards.body:
Stories in company, Chesterfield warned, are among the most tedious things there are. Tell one only when it is very apt and very short. Cut every detail that does not matter and beware of wandering off track. Leaning on stories all the time, he thought, shows a lack of imagination.

We all know the friend whose anecdote takes ten minutes and three detours. The fix is easy: know your point before you start, drop the scene-setting, and stop once you have made it. A tight story that fits the moment lands far better than a long one.
cards.quote: Tell stories very seldom, and absolutely never but where they are very apt and very short. Omit every circumstance that is not material, and beware of digressions.
cards.apply_it: Before you tell your next story, decide on its last line first. Then cut anything that does not lead there.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield say about details in a story?
options: Add as many as possible for colour
Omit every circumstance that is not material
quiz.explanation: He advised cutting every detail that does not matter and avoiding digressions.

cards.title: Take the mood of the room rather than setting it
cards.body:
Chesterfield told his son to take, rather than give, the tone of the company he was in: serious with the serious, cheerful with the cheerful, even light with those who are being light. He called this an attention each person owes to the group.

He was clear that this flexibility concerns manners, not morals. You are adapting your style, not your principles. Walking into a quiet office with loud weekend stories, or joking at a sombre gathering, jars. Reading the room first and joining it is simple courtesy.
cards.quote: Take, rather than give, the tone of the company you are in.
cards.apply_it: When you next arrive at a gathering, spend the first few minutes listening to catch its mood before you add your own.

quiz.question: According to Chesterfield, adapting to the tone of a company relates to what?
quiz.explanation: He said this kind of flexibility relates only to manners, not to morals.

cards.title: Stop advertising yourself: your real merit will be noticed
cards.body:
Above all, Chesterfield said, avoid speaking of yourself. He listed the ways vanity sneaks out: open boasting, complaining of imagined criticism so you can list your virtues, or confessing your 'weakness' of being too generous or too honest. People see through every one.

His cure was simple. Your character will become known whatever you do, and nobody takes it on your own word. Self-praise makes your faults more glaring and hides your strengths. Staying quiet about yourself lets the credit you deserve come freely from others.
cards.quote: Be your character what it will, it will be known; and nobody will take it upon your own word.
cards.apply_it: Notice the next time you are about to steer a conversation toward your own achievements, and ask the other person about theirs instead.

quiz.question: Why did Chesterfield think self-praise backfires?
options: People never take your character on your own word, and it makes faults more glaring
quiz.explanation: Your character becomes known anyway, and praising yourself tends to highlight your faults and hide your merits.

cards.title: Neither pass on gossip nor gladly receive it
cards.body:
Chesterfield's rule on scandal had two halves: do not spread it and do not welcome it. Running others down may give a moment's satisfaction, he admitted, but on cool reflection people judge harshly anyone who enjoys it.

He compared it to stolen goods: the person who receives scandal is thought as bad as the one who steals it. Today that includes forwarded screenshots and group-chat whispers. Changing the subject, or simply not reacting, quietly keeps you out of the trade.
cards.quote: in the case of scandal, as in that of robbery, the receiver is always thought, as bad as the thief.
cards.apply_it: The next time someone starts to share gossip, try a neutral reply such as 'I would rather hear it from them' and move on.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield compare receiving scandal to?
quiz.explanation: Like the receiver of stolen goods, whoever welcomes scandal is thought as bad as the one who spreads it.

cards.title: People may forgive a wrong, but they rarely forgive contempt
cards.body:
Chesterfield worried that his son showed too little attention to everybody and too much contempt to many. He warned that no one is so unimportant that they might not one day be able to help you, and they will not if you once looked down on them.

Wrongs are often forgiven, he said, but contempt never is, because pride remembers it. Contempt exposes weaknesses people guard more closely than their faults. He said the same of mimicking people: the person copied feels insulted. An eye-roll, a sneer or a mocking impression can outlast any argument.
cards.quote: Wrongs are often forgiven; but contempt never is. Our pride remembers it forever.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you tend to dismiss. Look for one thing they do well and tell them.

quiz.question: Why, according to Chesterfield, is contempt so rarely forgiven?
options: Because our pride remembers it forever
quiz.explanation: Contempt wounds pride and exposes weaknesses we would rather hide, so it is remembered long after a wrong is forgiven.

cards.title: When an argument stalls, agree to talk about something else
cards.body:
Never keep up an argument with heat and noise, Chesterfield advised, even when you know you are right. Give your view modestly and coolly, which he called the only way to convince anyone. And if that fails, change the subject with good humour.

He even offered the words: we shall hardly convince one another, nor is it necessary that we should, so let us talk of something else. Many family dinners and online threads would go better with that line. Not every disagreement needs a winner.
cards.quote: We shall hardly convince one another, nor is it necessary that we should, so let us talk of something else.
cards.apply_it: Keep Chesterfield's line ready in your own words for the next debate that starts going in circles.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield suggest when you cannot convince someone?
options: Change the subject with good humour
Bring more evidence until they give in
Leave the room without a word
quiz.explanation: He advised giving your view coolly and, if that fails, cheerfully moving to another topic.

cards.title: Soften how you disagree and your point gets stronger
cards.body:
Chesterfield did not want his son to be a pushover. Assert your own opinion, he said, and oppose others when they are wrong. But let your manner, words and tone be gentle. Use softening phrases when you contradict: I may be mistaken, I am not sure, but I believe, is it not rather so?

These words do not weaken an argument, he insisted. They make it more persuasive by making it more pleasant to hear. He also suggested ending a dispute with a little good-humoured remark, to show you are neither hurt nor trying to hurt.
cards.quote: Such mitigating, engaging words do by no means weaken your argument; but, on the contrary, make it more powerful by making it more pleasing.
cards.apply_it: Next time you disagree with someone, open with 'I might be wrong, but I see it this way' and notice how they respond.

quiz.question: What effect did Chesterfield say softening phrases have on an argument?
options: They make it more powerful by making it more pleasing
quiz.explanation: Gentle, modest wording makes a point easier to accept, so it persuades better.

cards.title: Wear your learning like a watch, in a private pocket
cards.body:
Chesterfield disliked pedants who scattered scraps of Latin to look clever. His advice: never seem wiser or more learned than the people you are with, and speak the plain language of the company.

His image is a good one. Keep your learning like a watch in your pocket. If someone asks the time, tell them. But do not pull it out and announce the hour unasked, like a night watchman. Today that might mean skipping the jargon, not correcting people for sport, and sharing what you know when it is wanted.
cards.quote: Wear your learning, like your watch, in a private pocket: and do not pull it out and strike it; merely to show that you have one.
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation outside your field, explain any specialist idea in everyday words, or leave it out.

quiz.question: When should you 'pull out the watch' of your learning, in Chesterfield's image?
quiz.explanation: If someone asks the time, tell them; otherwise keep your learning in your pocket.

cards.title: In the first flash of anger, stay silent until you can speak gently
cards.body:
Chesterfield admitted that some people have a hasty temper that bursts out in rough words to bosses, equals or juniors alike. His remedy was short: watch it closely, check it carefully, and when anger first flares, say nothing until you can say it gently.

He also urged learning to keep strong feelings from showing all over your face, which he called a great advantage in business. The pause is the key. A few breaths or a walk round the block before replying to the angry email can save a relationship.
cards.quote: at the first impulse of passion, be silent till you can be soft.
cards.apply_it: Decide now on your pause: the next time you feel anger rise, wait at least ten breaths before you speak or type.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield advise at the first impulse of anger?
options: Say exactly what you feel at once
Be silent till you can be soft
quiz.explanation: He advised staying silent until you could speak gently, rather than letting the first heat speak for you.

cards.title: Be gentle in manner and firm in substance
cards.body:
Chesterfield's favourite rule was a Latin phrase, suaviter in modo, fortiter in re: gentle in manner, firm in the matter. He thought each half failed without the other. Gentleness alone sinks into timid, people-pleasing passiveness. Firmness alone turns harsh and makes people hate you.

The hot-tempered person who pushes through on force usually fails, he said, and the crafty one who agrees with everyone is soon found out. The wise person joins the two: kind in tone, steady in what they will and will not do. He called the pair a short but full description of human perfection.
cards.quote: gentleness of manners, with firmness of mind, is a short, but full description of human perfection on this side of religious and moral duties.
cards.apply_it: Think of a request you need to hold firm on. Write down the gentlest possible words you could use to say it.

quiz.question: What happens to gentleness without firmness, in Chesterfield's view?
options: It sinks into timid complaisance and passiveness
quiz.explanation: Gentleness without firmness becomes weak people-pleasing; firmness without gentleness becomes brutality.

cards.title: Give instructions kindly and they will be carried out willingly
cards.body:
Applying his gentle-but-firm rule to authority, Chesterfield said that commands given gently are obeyed willingly, cheerfully and therefore well. Commands given roughly are more likely to be resisted than carried out.

He gave a homely example. If he ordered his servant to bring a glass of wine in a rough, insulting way, he would expect some of it to be spilled on him, and he would deserve it. A calm firmness should make clear you expect to be obeyed, while a gentle manner softens the sting of being told what to do. Good managers still work this way.
cards.quote: A cool, steady resolution should show that where you have a right to command you will be obeyed
cards.apply_it: Rewrite one instruction you need to give this week so it is clear about what is needed and warm in how it is asked.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield expect if he gave his servant a rough, insulting order?
options: That some wine would be spilled on him, deservedly
quiz.explanation: He joked that harsh orders invite quiet resistance, and that he would deserve the spilled wine.

cards.title: Do not assume the laughter in the room is about you
cards.body:
Chesterfield noticed that people new to a social setting often imagine they are the centre of attention. If people whisper, it must be about them; if they laugh, it must be at them. Soon they feel embarrassed, then angry.

A well-bred person, he said, rarely thinks and never seems to think that they are being slighted or laughed at, unless it is unmistakable. Most of the time other people are thinking about themselves. Giving the benefit of the doubt saves you a lot of needless hurt.
cards.quote: A well-bred man seldom thinks, but never seems to think himself slighted, undervalued, or laughed at in company
cards.apply_it: Next time you suspect a remark was aimed at you, list two other likely explanations before you react.

quiz.question: How do people new to company often misread laughter, according to Chesterfield?
options: They think it is always friendly
They think it is rude to laugh
They think it is aimed at them
quiz.explanation: Self-conscious newcomers tend to imagine every whisper or laugh is about them, then grow embarrassed and angry.

cards.title: Never snub an old friend to impress fashionable company
cards.body:
Chesterfield confessed a regret. As a young man he sometimes greeted an unglamorous acquaintance shyly and awkwardly when he was with 'fine' people, afraid of a passing joke. He realised later that those same people would have respected him more for being warm.

If he met such a friend now, he said, he would go straight up, embrace him, say something kind, and laugh off any teasing afterwards. Being ashamed of doing the right thing for fear of a moment's mockery, he wrote, loses you friends and gains you enemies.
cards.quote: They are ashamed of doing the thing they know to be right, and would otherwise do, for fear of the momentary laugh of some fine gentleman or lady
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you have held at arm's length in front of others. Greet them warmly the next time you see them.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield say he would now do on meeting an unfashionable old friend in elegant company?
options: Go up, embrace him and say something kind
quiz.explanation: He said he would greet the friend warmly and laugh off any teasing, since people respect that loyalty.

cards.title: Laugh at your own mistakes first and others will not laugh at you
cards.body:
Sending his son to Rome, Chesterfield told him to speak Italian to everyone, right or wrong. If he laughed at himself first for his bad Italian, nobody else would laugh at him. That, he said, was the only way to learn to speak it well.

The lesson reaches beyond languages. When you are learning anything in public, from a new sport to a new job, owning your clumsiness with a smile takes the sting out of mistakes and gives you the freedom to keep practising.
cards.quote: Speak Italian, right or wrong, to everybody; and if you do but laugh at yourself first for your bad Italian, nobody else will laugh at you for it.
cards.apply_it: Try out something you are still learning in front of others this week, and name your beginner status cheerfully as you do.

quiz.question: Why did Chesterfield want his son to speak Italian 'right or wrong'?
options: Because practising, and laughing at his own errors, was the only way to speak it well
quiz.explanation: Speaking freely and laughing at his own mistakes first was the route to speaking well.

cards.title: In-jokes rarely survive being moved to a new crowd
cards.body:
The wit and jokes of any group, Chesterfield observed, are local. They grow in that particular soil but seldom bear transplanting. Every circle has its own references and shorthand, which are funny inside it and flat anywhere else.

Nothing looks sillier, he said, than a joke met with silence, unless it is being asked to explain it. Today that covers office banter retold at home and group-chat memes shared with strangers. Before you repeat something that was hilarious elsewhere, ask whether this audience has the context to enjoy it.
cards.quote: Remember that the wit, humor, and jokes, of most mixed companies are local. They thrive in that particular soil, but will not often bear transplanting.
cards.apply_it: Before retelling a joke or story from another group, ask: will these people know enough to find it funny?

quiz.question: Why do jokes from one group often fall flat in another?
options: Each group has its own references that outsiders lack
quiz.explanation: Humour often depends on a group's shared context, so it rarely transplants well.

cards.title: What is said in one company should stay there
cards.body:
Chesterfield warned his son never to repeat in one group what he heard in another. Things that seem harmless can have serious consequences once they circulate. And he described an unspoken agreement in all conversation: you do not carry things out of it, even when nobody has asked you to keep a secret.

Those who pass things along, he said, get into endless scrapes and find people uneasy around them. In an age of screenshots and forwarding, the tacit trust he described matters more than ever.
cards.quote: there is a general tacit trust in conversation, by which a man is obliged not to report anything out of it, though he is not immediately enjoined to secrecy.
cards.apply_it: Before you forward a message or retell a conversation, ask whether the person who said it would be comfortable with that.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield say about repeating conversations when no one has asked for secrecy?
options: It is fine if not forbidden
There is a tacit trust not to report things anyway
Only repeat it to close friends
Repeat it if it is interesting
quiz.explanation: He described an unspoken trust in conversation: you do not carry things out of it, even without being asked.

cards.title: Keep your hopes and plans to yourself until they are settled
cards.body:
Chesterfield repeatedly told his son to keep his own secrets, adding that very few people can. Writing about a hoped-for appointment, he advised telling no one, because a disappointment always carries some ridicule, even when the hope was reasonable.

It is prudent, he wrote, not to share your hopes or your fears too early. Announcing the job you have applied for or the plan not yet confirmed invites questions if it falls through, and can even make it harder to pull off. Let results speak when they arrive.
cards.quote: it is certainly most prudent not to communicate, prematurely, one’s hopes or one’s fears.
cards.apply_it: Pick one plan you are working on and decide to keep it to yourself until it is settled.

quiz.question: Why did Chesterfield advise not announcing your hopes early?
options: It is against good manners to hope
A disappointment attracts some ridicule, even if the hope was reasonable
quiz.explanation: If a publicly announced hope fails, there is often some ridicule, even when the expectation was reasonable.

cards.title: Notice how long you are welcome, and leave a little before
cards.body:
A sensible person, Chesterfield wrote, soon discovers where and how long they are welcome, because they pay attention. Then they take care to leave at least as soon as people start wishing them gone. Fools, he added, never notice when they are badly timed or out of place.

The signs are usually there: glances at the clock, shorter replies, a host starting to tidy. Leaving while the mood is still good is a quiet gift to your hosts, and it makes them glad to see you again.
cards.quote: A man of sense soon discovers, because he carefully observes, where, and how long, he is welcome; and takes care to leave the company, at least as soon as he is wished out of it.
cards.apply_it: At your next visit or call, watch for the first sign that people are ready to wrap up, and be the one to end it warmly.

quiz.question: How does a sensible person know when to leave, according to Chesterfield?
options: By a fixed rule of one hour
By carefully observing where and how long they are welcome
quiz.explanation: Close observation shows how long you are welcome, so you can leave before you are wished away.

cards.title: Flattery cheapens you as much as constant contradiction
cards.body:
Chesterfield's art of pleasing did not mean saying yes to everything. He warned that grovelling flattery and agreeing with whatever is said degrade a person, just as contradicting everything and arguing noisily disgusts people.

The dignified middle, he wrote, is to state your own view modestly and to accept other people's views graciously where you can. You can be pleasant without pretending. People trust the praise of someone who does not hand it out to everyone.
cards.quote: But a modest assertion of one’s own opinion, and a complaisant acquiescence to other people’s, preserve dignity.
cards.apply_it: The next time you are tempted to agree just to please, say what you genuinely think in one modest sentence.

quiz.question: What preserves dignity, in Chesterfield's view?
options: Modestly asserting your view and graciously accepting others'
quiz.explanation: Neither flattery nor constant contradiction works; modest honesty plus graciousness keeps your dignity.

cards.title: Speak to people below you without arrogance and above you without fear
cards.body:
Chesterfield described awkward people who, meeting someone important, fumble their hats and forget where their hands go. The well-bred person, he said, talks with those beneath them without insolence and with those above them with respect and ease.

The test cuts both ways. How you treat the junior colleague, the cleaner or the waiter says as much about you as how you handle the chief executive. Steady, equal courtesy in both directions is what people come to trust in a leader.
cards.quote: The characteristic of a well-bred man, is to converse with his inferiors without insolence, and with his superiors with respect and ease.
cards.apply_it: This week, give the same full attention to the most junior person you deal with as you would to your manager.

quiz.question: How should a well-bred person speak to people of higher standing, according to Chesterfield?
quiz.explanation: He described ease and respect toward superiors, and no insolence toward those below.

cards.title: Whatever is worth doing at all is worth doing well
cards.body:
Chesterfield wrote this famous line to his son early on. Nothing can be done well without attention, he said, and he applied that to the smallest things, even dancing and dress. If you must do something, mind it while you learn it, so you do it well and are not ridiculous.

The principle works today for the emails, reports and chores that seem beneath full effort. A task done with care saves you redoing it, and small things done well build a reputation for doing big things well.
cards.quote: In truth, whatever is worth doing at all, is worth doing well; and nothing can be done well without attention
cards.apply_it: Pick one routine task today and give it your full attention from start to finish, as if someone you admire would see it.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield say is required to do anything well?
quiz.explanation: He said nothing can be done well without attention, even the smallest things.

cards.title: Move quickly when needed, but never in a flap
cards.body:
Chesterfield drew a sharp line between haste and hurry. A sensible person can be in haste, moving fast because the task needs it. But someone in a hurry, he said, shows that the thing they are doing is too big for them.

Hurry is the flustered, scattered rush that drops things and spreads panic to others. Haste is speed with a clear head. When pressure mounts, slow your breathing, decide on the next single step and take it. You will often finish faster than if you had rushed.
cards.quote: Whoever is in a hurry, shows that the thing he is about is too big for him. Haste and hurry are very different things.
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel rushed, stop for ten seconds, name the very next step, and do only that.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield say being 'in a hurry' reveals?
options: That the task is too big for you
quiz.explanation: Hurry signals being overwhelmed; haste is simply moving quickly with composure.

cards.title: Use a simple method for everything and stick to it
cards.body:
Dispatch is the soul of business, Chesterfield wrote, and nothing helps dispatch like method. He advised fixing one hour on one day each week for going through accounts, so they take little time and nobody can cheat you. Letters and papers should be labelled and filed by type, so you can find any one at once.

He also suggested rising at the same hour each morning to secure an hour or two before the day's interruptions begin. A weekly money check, a simple filing system and a protected morning hour remain solid foundations.
cards.quote: Dispatch is the soul of business; and nothing contributes more to dispatch than method.
cards.apply_it: Choose one fixed hour each week to review your money and paperwork, and put it in your calendar now.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield advise for keeping accounts?
options: Check them only at year end
Let someone else handle them entirely
Fix one certain hour and day each week for them
quiz.explanation: A fixed weekly time keeps accounts quick to manage and protects you from being cheated.

cards.title: Write so clearly that nobody can misread you
cards.body:
For business letters, Chesterfield said the first need is extreme clearness. Every paragraph should be so plain that the dullest reader could not mistake it or need to read it twice. Clever turns of phrase and showy figures of speech are out of place.

His editing method still works: after writing each paragraph, reread it looking for any way it could be misunderstood, and fix it. Emails, briefs and instructions save everyone time when they pass this test.
cards.quote: every paragraph should be so clear and unambiguous, that the dullest fellow in the world may not be able to mistake it, nor obliged to read it twice in order to understand it.
cards.apply_it: Before sending your next important email, reread each paragraph asking: could anyone take this the wrong way?

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield say is the first thing needed in a business letter?
quiz.explanation: Clarity comes first in business writing, so no reader can mistake the meaning.

cards.title: How you say it decides whether people listen
cards.body:
Chesterfield watched speakers in Parliament closely. One lord argued with knowledge but spoke clumsily, and nobody listened. Another, the Duke of Argyle, reasoned weakly but spoke so gracefully that he carried the room. Chesterfield admitted he too was captivated, until he got home and found the arguments flimsy.

His conclusion was two-sided. To be heard well, you must be pleasant to hear: choose words carefully and speak clearly. And as a listener, remember how much delivery can sway you, and weigh the content afterwards.
cards.quote: To be heard with success, you must be heard with pleasure: words are the dress of thoughts
cards.apply_it: Record yourself explaining an idea for one minute. Listen back and fix one thing about your clarity or pace.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield discover about the Duke of Argyle's speeches when he thought them over at home?
options: They were even better than he thought
quiz.explanation: Argyle's delivery was captivating, but his reasoning was weak, which showed the power of manner.

cards.title: Do not accept a claim just because an author made it
cards.body:
Chesterfield encouraged his son's careful way of reading history. Take nothing for granted on the bare authority of the author, he wrote. Weigh how likely the facts are and whether the reflections are sound.

He also advised consulting several authors on the same events and forming your own view from the whole. This is exactly how to read news and online claims today: check more than one source, ask whether the story is probable, and treat a confident tone as no proof.
cards.quote: take nothing for granted, upon the bare authority of the author; but weigh and consider, in your own mind, the probability of the facts and the justness of the reflections.
cards.apply_it: The next time a striking claim crosses your feed, find two other sources before you believe or share it.

quiz.question: How did Chesterfield suggest forming an opinion on historical facts?
options: Consult different authors and weigh the probabilities
quiz.explanation: He recommended comparing several authors and judging by the overall probability.

cards.title: Question the opinions you picked up without examining them
cards.body:
In an unusually candid letter, Chesterfield confessed that for years he simply adopted the views of the books he read and the people he kept company with, never checking whether they were right. Laziness, distraction and the embarrassment of rejecting fashionable ideas kept him there.

When he finally began reasoning for himself, many of his views changed. He even admitted some old errors might remain, because habits learned early are hard to tell apart from real conclusions. It is a humble model for checking your own inherited opinions.
cards.quote: I adopted the notions of the books I read, or the company I kept, without examining whether they were just or not
cards.apply_it: Pick one strong opinion you hold and write down where you first got it. Then look for the best argument against it.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield admit about his early opinions?
options: He took them from books and company without examining them
He reasoned them all out carefully
He inherited them from his father only
quiz.explanation: He confessed he had absorbed views from books and friends without checking them, until he learned to reason for himself.

cards.title: The best have flaws and the worst have good in them
cards.body:
Reading history taught Chesterfield that people are inconsistent. Moods, passions and circumstances make everyone more 'the man of the day' than a fixed character. He distrusted historians who described anyone as all good or all bad.

Elsewhere he advised never adopting someone's character purely on common reputation, which is right in outline but wrong in particulars. Look for yourself. This is a useful brake on hero worship and on writing people off. Most people are a mix, and seeing that helps you deal with them fairly.
cards.quote: The best have something bad, and something little; the worst have something good, and sometimes something great
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you strongly dislike and name one genuinely good thing about them.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield believe about human character?
options: People are consistent all their lives
The best have flaws and the worst have some good
quiz.explanation: He saw people as mixed and changeable: even the best have faults, and even the worst have good in them.

cards.title: Half-knowing something is often worse than not knowing it
cards.body:
Chesterfield urged his son to go to the bottom of things. Whatever you do, do it thoroughly, not superficially. Anything half done or half known, he said, is neither done nor known at all, and worse, it often misleads.

This is a fair warning for an age of headlines and quick summaries. A partial understanding can make us confident and wrong. When something matters, keep going until you can explain it simply in your own words, including why it is so.
cards.quote: Any thing half done or half known, is, in my mind, neither done nor known at all. Nay worse, it often misleads.
cards.apply_it: Choose one topic you only half understand. Spend twenty minutes on it today until you can explain it to a friend.

quiz.question: Why did Chesterfield think half-knowledge could be worse than none?
quiz.explanation: Knowing something only partly can mislead you, which may be worse than knowing you do not know.

cards.title: Everyone you meet can teach you something
cards.body:
When his son found some companions dull, Chesterfield told him not to show contempt or mock them, which was against good sense as well as good manners. Instead, get all the good you can out of them, since something can be learned from everybody. Ask them about what they know.

He noted that almost everyone knows one thing well and is glad to talk about it. Asking a neighbour about their trade or a colleague about their home country turns a dull chat into a lesson, and makes them feel valued too.
cards.quote: endeavor rather to get all the good you can out of them; and something or other is to be got out of everybody.
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation with someone you find dull, ask them about something they know well and listen.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield advise instead of mocking dull companions?
options: Get all the good you can out of them
quiz.explanation: He said something can be learned from everybody, so draw out what they know.

cards.title: Ask when you do not understand, even if it feels awkward
cards.body:
Chesterfield urged his son to state his difficulties whenever he had any, and not to hide them out of false shame, laziness, or a wish to be done sooner. In lectures, he said, let nothing pass until you are sure you understand it thoroughly.

The instinct to nod along is strong in classrooms and meetings alike. But a confusion left unasked tends to grow. One clear question now usually saves hours of muddle later, and often helps others who were too shy to ask.
cards.quote: State your difficulties, whenever you have any; and do not suppress them, either from mistaken shame, lazy indifference, or in order to have done the sooner.
cards.apply_it: In your next meeting or class, ask one clarifying question about anything you did not fully follow.

quiz.question: Which reason for hiding difficulties did Chesterfield mention?
quiz.explanation: He listed mistaken shame, lazy indifference and wanting to finish sooner as poor reasons for staying silent.

cards.title: You will rise or sink to the level of the company you keep
cards.body:
Chesterfield warned that vanity leads some people to choose company beneath them, just to be the star of a small circle. That comfort comes at a price. You will sink or rise to the level of the people you usually spend time with, he wrote, and others will judge you by them.

He quoted a Spanish saying: tell me whom you live with, and I will tell you who you are. Seek out people who stretch you, even if it means you are no longer the most impressive person in the room.
cards.quote: Depend upon it, you will sink or rise to the level of the company which you commonly keep
cards.apply_it: List the five people you spend most time with. Note one way each lifts you, and one person you would like to see more of.

quiz.question: Why do some people choose company beneath them, according to Chesterfield?
options: Out of vanity, to be the first person in it
quiz.explanation: Vanity draws people to circles where they can be the star, but that holds them back.

cards.title: Real friendship grows slowly
cards.body:
Chesterfield warned his son against 'friendships' offered at first sight. Receive them with civility, he said, but also with doubt; pay them in compliments, not confidences. Do not let vanity convince you that people become true friends on short acquaintance.

Real friendship, he wrote, is a slow grower and thrives only on known, mutual worth. He also urged a clear distinction between companions and friends, since an agreeable companion may make a poor friend. Enjoy new acquaintances, but let trust build over time.
cards.quote: Real friendship is a slow grower and never thrives unless engrafted upon a stock of known and reciprocal merit.
cards.apply_it: Think of a new acquaintance you have quickly confided in. Ask yourself what you actually know of their character so far.

quiz.question: How should you respond to instant offers of friendship, according to Chesterfield?
options: With civility, but also with incredulity
quiz.explanation: He advised courtesy combined with caution, repaying them with compliments but not confidences.

cards.title: Have opinions of your own and hold them with good humour
cards.body:
Chesterfield described a type found in every group: the 'very good-natured fellow' who has no will of his own and cheerfully agrees with whatever the majority says, wise or foolish, right or wrong. He thought this a contemptible way to keep your place.

His advice was to have a will and an opinion of your own and stick to them, but with good humour and courtesy. He added a gentle caution for the young: you have not yet seen enough either to preach or to condemn. Conviction and kindness can go together.
cards.quote: Have a will and an opinion of your own, and adhere to them steadily; but then do it with good humor, good-breeding
cards.apply_it: Next time a group heads toward a decision you disagree with, state your view calmly in one sentence.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield criticise in the 'very good-natured fellow'?
options: He has no will of his own and agrees with everything
quiz.explanation: Such people simply echo the majority, good or bad, instead of holding views of their own.

cards.title: To a loving parent, your small news is never small
cards.body:
Chesterfield, who disliked people talking about themselves, made one exception. He asked his son to fill his letters with himself, the one place egotism was welcome. Trifles that concern you, he wrote, are not trifles to me, and knowing them might help me to help you.

It is a tender reminder for parents, and for anyone who loves someone. The small details of a child's day are how you stay close and notice when something is wrong. Ask about them, and let them matter to you.
cards.quote: Trifles that concern you are not trifles to me; and my knowledge of them may possibly be useful to you.
cards.apply_it: Ask someone you love about one small, ordinary part of their day, and listen as if it is the most important news you will hear.

quiz.question: Where did Chesterfield welcome egotism?
options: In his son's letters to him
quiz.explanation: He asked his son to make his letters full of himself, because the details of his life mattered to his father.

cards.title: We need others to show us our faults, because self-love hides them
cards.body:
After pointing out some of his son's faults, Chesterfield explained why. Hardly anyone else would care enough to notice and correct them, so the boy might never know. Our own self-love, he wrote, draws a thick veil between us and our faults.

He hoped that his care as a father would one day give way to that of a friend. Honest feedback from someone who wants only your good is rare. Parents can offer it gently, and all of us can welcome it rather than bristle.
cards.quote: for our own self-love draws a thick veil between us and our faults.
cards.apply_it: Ask someone who has your interests at heart: what is one habit of mine you think holds me back?

quiz.question: Why did Chesterfield say his son might otherwise never know his faults?
options: Because his tutor was too strict
Because self-love veils them and few others would care to point them out
quiz.explanation: Self-love hides our faults from us, and few people care enough to tell us.

cards.title: Do not raise a child to think the world was made for them
cards.body:
Chesterfield wrote sharply about a couple who, he said, had ruined their son by what they thought was love. They had taught him that the world was made for him, not he for the world. Out in life he would expect from strangers the endless attention he had always had at home, and he would not find it.

Chesterfield said he had tried instead to help his son deserve affection. Loving a child includes preparing them to give as well as receive.
cards.quote: They have made him believe that the world was made for him, not he for the world
cards.apply_it: Find one small way this week to let a child in your life contribute to others, such as a chore, a kindness or a thank-you.

quiz.question: What mistake did Chesterfield say these parents made?
options: They taught their son the world was made for him
They gave him too many books
quiz.explanation: By indulging him completely, they left him expecting attention he would never find outside home.

cards.title: Learn to tell what is impossible from what is only difficult
cards.body:
Telling a story of a diplomat who calmly persisted until he won a point everyone thought hopeless, Chesterfield drew a lesson. Good sense must distinguish what is truly impossible from what is only difficult. Spirit and perseverance will overcome the difficult.

Elsewhere he urged his son to let difficulties sharpen his efforts rather than slacken them, adding that perseverance has surprising effects. Many goals that feel impossible are just hard. Sorting the two honestly tells you where steady effort will pay off.
cards.quote: Sense must distinguish between what is impossible, and what is only difficult; and spirit and perseverance will get the better of the latter.
cards.apply_it: Take a goal you have filed under 'impossible'. Write down exactly what makes it hard, and one step that would chip at it.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield say spirit and perseverance can overcome?
quiz.explanation: Perseverance conquers the merely difficult; good sense is needed to tell that apart from the truly impossible.

cards.title: Say no gracefully and people will feel better than at a clumsy yes
cards.body:
Manner, Chesterfield argued, often matters more than the thing itself. He put it memorably: better to refuse a favour gracefully than to grant it clumsily. He advised special gentleness whenever you must refuse a request or deliver unwelcome news, calling it the gilding on a bitter pill.

A warm, clear no with thanks and a reason leaves the relationship intact. A grudging yes with a sigh can leave the other person feeling worse than a refusal would.
cards.quote: you had better refuse a favor gracefully, than to grant it clumsily.
cards.apply_it: Next time you must decline a request, thank the person, give a brief honest reason, and wish them well.

quiz.question: What did Chesterfield say about refusing favours?
options: Better to refuse gracefully than grant clumsily
quiz.explanation: A graceful refusal can leave someone feeling better than a grudging yes.

cards.title: Thank people warmly and quickly, not late and lukewarm
cards.body:
When a friend went out of his way to help his son into Parliament, Chesterfield told him to write a letter of thanks by the very next post. And he described the kind of thanks he wanted: warm and young, not old and cold.

Gratitude loses its glow when it arrives weeks late or sounds like duty. A prompt message that names exactly what the person did and why it mattered is one of the best small investments in any relationship.
cards.quote: write him a letter of thanks, warm and young thanks, not old and cold ones.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who helped you recently. Send them a specific thank-you today.

quiz.question: What kind of thanks did Chesterfield want his son to send?
options: Warm and young, not old and cold
quiz.explanation: He wanted prompt, heartfelt thanks rather than late, dutiful ones.
